questions.text: What is the decimal value of the binary number (1011.11)<sub>2</sub>?
questions.solution: The integer part 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. The fraction .11 is 1/2 + 1/4 = 0.75. Together, 11.75.

questions.text: How many 1s are there in the binary representation of the decimal number 45?
questions.solution: 45 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 101101 in binary, which has four 1s.

questions.text: The hexadecimal number (2C)<sub>16</sub> is equal to which octal number?
questions.solution: 2C hex is 2 x 16 + 12 = 44 decimal. Going to octal, 44 = 5 x 8 + 4, so (54) octal. Going through binary is quicker: 2C = 0010 1100 = 101100, grouped in threes as 101 100 = 54.

questions.text: How many bits are needed to represent the decimal number 1000 in unsigned binary?
questions.solution: 2^9 = 512 is too small and 2^10 = 1024 is enough, so 10 bits. In general the count is floor(log2 N) + 1.

questions.text: What is the 8-bit 2's complement representation of the negative of 00010110?
questions.solution: Invert every bit to get the 1's complement, 11101001, then add 1 to get 11101010. Option B is the 1's complement, which is the usual slip.

questions.text: What is the range of integers representable in 8-bit 2's complement form?
questions.solution: 2's complement has a single representation of zero, so the negative side reaches one further than the positive: -2^7 to 2^7 - 1. The symmetric range -127 to +127 belongs to 1's complement, which has two zeros.

questions.text: Interpreted as an 8-bit 2's complement number, what decimal value does 11111011 represent?
questions.solution: The leading 1 marks it negative. Invert to 00000100 and add 1, giving 00000101 = 5, so the value is -5.

questions.text: What is the Gray code equivalent of the binary number 1010?
questions.solution: Keep the most significant bit, then XOR each bit with the one to its left: g3 = 1, g2 = 1 XOR 0 = 1, g1 = 0 XOR 1 = 1, g0 = 1 XOR 0 = 1, giving 1111.

questions.text: What property makes Gray code useful for position encoders and K-map ordering?

options.text: Consecutive code words differ in exactly one bit
It needs fewer bits than binary

questions.solution: Only one bit changes between neighbours, so a reading taken mid-transition can be off by at most one position. Gray code is unweighted and uses exactly as many bits as binary.

questions.text: The Gray code word 1110 corresponds to which binary number?
questions.solution: Gray to binary runs left to right, each binary bit being the XOR of the previous binary bit with the current Gray bit: b3 = 1, b2 = 1 XOR 1 = 0, b1 = 0 XOR 1 = 1, b0 = 1 XOR 0 = 1, giving 1011.

questions.text: What is the 4-bit Gray code for decimal 6?
questions.solution: Decimal 6 is 0110 in binary. XOR each bit with the one to its left: 0, 0 XOR 1 = 1, 1 XOR 1 = 0, 1 XOR 0 = 1, giving 0101.

questions.text: In IEEE 754 single precision, how many bits are allotted to the exponent field?
questions.solution: Single precision splits 32 bits into 1 sign, 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits. Double precision uses 11 exponent bits.

questions.text: How many fraction (mantissa) bits are stored in an IEEE 754 single precision number?
questions.solution: 23 bits are stored. The precision is effectively 24 bits because a normalised number has an implicit leading 1 that is never written down.

questions.text: What is the exponent bias used in IEEE 754 single precision?
questions.solution: With 8 exponent bits the bias is 2^7 - 1 = 127, so a stored exponent of 128 means an actual exponent of 1. The bias lets exponents be compared as unsigned integers. 1023 is the double precision bias.

questions.text: The Boolean expression A + AB simplifies to which of the following?
questions.solution: By absorption, A + AB = A(1 + B) = A. Whenever A is 1 the expression is 1 regardless of B, and when A is 0 both terms are 0.

questions.text: The Boolean expression A + A'B simplifies to which of the following?
questions.solution: A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) = A + B. The complemented literal is absorbed, which is easy to confuse with plain absorption where the answer would be just A.

questions.text: According to De Morgan's theorem, (A . B)' is equal to which of the following?
questions.solution: Complementing a product gives the sum of the complements: the NAND of A and B is the OR of their inverses. A' . B' is the complement of A + B, which is the other half of the theorem.

questions.text: The expression AB + AB' simplifies to which of the following?
questions.solution: AB + AB' = A(B + B') = A . 1 = A. B appears in both polarities and so cannot affect the result.

questions.text: The product-of-sums expression (A + B)(A + B') simplifies to which of the following?
questions.solution: Expanding gives AA + AB' + AB + BB' = A + A(B + B') + 0 = A. It is the dual of AB + AB' = A.

questions.text: How many literals appear in the minimal sum-of-products form of F = AB + ABC + AB' ?
questions.solution: ABC is covered by AB, so F = AB + AB' = A(B + B') = A. The minimal form is the single literal A.

questions.text: F(A, B, C) = sum of minterms m(0, 1, 2, 3). What is the minimal expression?
questions.solution: Minterms 0 to 3 are exactly the rows where A = 0, with B and C taking every combination. They merge into the single cube A'.

questions.text: F(A, B, C, D) = sum of minterms m(0, 2, 8, 10). What is the minimal expression?
questions.solution: The four minterms are 0000, 0010, 1000 and 1010. A and C take both values while B = 0 and D = 0 throughout, so the group of four reduces to B'D'.

questions.text: F(A, B, C) = sum of minterms m(1, 3, 5, 7). What is the minimal expression?
questions.solution: The odd minterms are precisely those with C = 1, and A and B range freely over them, so the function is just C.

questions.text: Which of the following is a universal gate?
questions.solution: NAND (and NOR) can implement NOT, AND and OR, and therefore any Boolean function. AND and OR alone cannot produce a complement.

questions.text: The output of a two-input XOR gate is 1 when
questions.solution: XOR is the inequality detector: it outputs 1 exactly when its inputs differ, which is why it also acts as a controllable inverter.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of two-input NAND gates required to implement a NOT gate?
questions.solution: Tie both inputs of a NAND together: (A . A)' = A'. One gate is enough.

questions.text: The output of a two-input XNOR gate is 1 when
questions.solution: XNOR is the complement of XOR, so it is the equality detector: 1 for 00 and 11, 0 otherwise.

questions.text: In a half adder with inputs A and B, the carry output is given by
questions.solution: A carry is produced only when both bits are 1, which is the AND. The sum output is A XOR B.

questions.text: How many half adders are needed to build one full adder (together with a single OR gate)?
questions.solution: The first half adder adds A and B, the second adds that sum to the carry-in, and an OR gate combines the two carries.

questions.text: For a full adder with inputs A, B and carry-in C, the sum output is
questions.solution: The sum bit is 1 when an odd number of the three inputs is 1, which is exactly the three-input XOR.

questions.text: How many full adders are required to build a 4-bit ripple carry adder?
questions.solution: One full adder per bit position, with each carry-out feeding the next stage's carry-in.

questions.text: For a full adder with inputs A, B and carry-in C, the carry-out is
questions.solution: A carry is generated when both A and B are 1, or propagated when exactly one of them is 1 and a carry comes in. This generate-propagate split is what carry look-ahead exploits.

questions.text: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 multiplexer have?
questions.solution: n select lines choose among 2^n inputs, so 8 inputs need 3 select lines.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of 4-to-1 multiplexers required to build a 16-to-1 multiplexer?
questions.solution: Four multiplexers in the first stage handle the 16 inputs in groups of four, and a fifth selects among their outputs: 5 in total.

questions.text: For a 2-to-1 multiplexer with inputs I0 and I1 and select line S, the output is
questions.solution: S = 0 selects I0 and S = 1 selects I1, so each input is gated by the matching polarity of the select line.

questions.text: How many outputs does a 3-to-8 decoder have?
questions.solution: A decoder asserts exactly one output per input combination, so n inputs give 2^n outputs: 8 here.

questions.text: How many output bits does an encoder with 16 inputs produce?
questions.solution: An encoder is the inverse of a decoder: 2^n inputs are coded into n outputs, and 16 = 2^4 gives 4.

questions.text: In a JK flip-flop, what happens when J = K = 1?
questions.solution: The JK flip-flop replaces the forbidden SR state with toggling, which is what makes it the building block of counters.

questions.text: The characteristic equation of a D flip-flop is
questions.solution: The D flip-flop simply captures its input at the clock edge, so the next state equals D regardless of the present state. That is why it is used for registers.

questions.text: The race-around condition in a level-triggered JK flip-flop occurs when

options.text: J = K = 1 and the clock pulse is wider than the propagation delay

questions.solution: With both inputs high the output toggles, and if the clock stays high longer than the propagation delay it toggles repeatedly, leaving the final state uncertain. Master-slave or edge triggering fixes it.

questions.text: How many flip-flops are required to build a mod-10 counter?
questions.solution: n flip-flops give 2^n states, and 10 states need 2^n >= 10, so n = 4. Six of the sixteen states go unused.

questions.text: A 4-bit binary ripple counter counts through which range before repeating?
questions.solution: Four bits hold 16 distinct states, from 0000 to 1111, that is 0 to 15.

questions.text: A ripple counter is called asynchronous because

options.text: each flip-flop is clocked by the output of the preceding one
it has no clock at all
its flip-flops change at random times

questions.solution: Only the first stage sees the external clock; the rest are triggered in turn, so the change ripples through and delays accumulate stage by stage. That accumulation limits the maximum counting speed.

questions.text: In a synchronous counter, the flip-flops

options.text: all receive the same clock signal simultaneously

questions.solution: A common clock means every stage changes at the same edge, so the settling delay is that of one flip-flop rather than the sum along the chain. Combinational logic on the inputs decides which stages toggle.

questions.text: What is the maximum modulus of a counter built from 5 flip-flops?
questions.solution: Five flip-flops hold 2^5 = 32 distinct states, so the largest possible modulus is 32.
